doctrine:
**Malversation (Art. 217, RPC).** Under the last paragraph of Article 217, an accountable public officer's failure to have public funds duly forthcoming upon demand by a duly authorized officer is prima facie evidence that the officer put them to personal use. This is a presumption of law that shifts the burden to the accused to rebut it with satisfactory evidence (reiterated, citing *Wa-acon v. People*). **Notwithstanding the stated purpose or intention for public funds to be applied for a public purpose, the presumption of malversation remains unrebutted absent proof that the funds were actually applied for that purpose.** A memorandum of agreement and sanggunian resolutions declaring that loans to local officials are for buying official service vehicles do not prove that the vehicles were bought and used for official purposes.

**Section 3(e), RA 3019.** Mere bad faith or partiality and negligence per se are not enough; the bad faith or partiality must be "evident" or "manifest" (reiterated, citing *Sistoza v. Desierto*). Evident bad faith connotes not only bad judgment but a "palpably and patently fraudulent and dishonest purpose to do moral obliquity or conscious wrongdoing for some perverse motive or ill will." **Local officials who, having no legal officer, acted on the opinion of the resident COA auditor that their fund realignment and loan scheme was legal did not act with evident bad faith.** They could presume the auditor performed his functions regularly and correctly, even though the opinion was verbal and given before audit. A finding that they "should have known better" shows ignorance, not evident bad faith.

Manifest partiality, evident bad faith, and gross inexcusable negligence **must be alleged with particularity in the Information**. The accused cannot be convicted on a modality that was not alleged (here, gross inexcusable negligence) or one the trial court made no finding on (here, manifest partiality).
facts:
Herminio Casal Reyes was the municipal mayor of Loreto, Agusan del Sur; Daday, Gomez, Estil, Plaza, Magadan and Julao were members of the Sangguniang Bayan (SB). In early 2003, citing an urgent need for service vehicles, SB member Gomez and SB Secretary Irisari proposed that the municipality lend money to its officials to buy motorcycles for exclusively official use. The money would come from the idle budget for the municipal building, whose construction had been suspended. Irisari consulted the resident COA auditor, Lorete, who verbally opined that the realignment was legal as long as the required documents were complied with and it was supported by an SB resolution. The municipality had no legal officer.

In March 2003, the municipality and its officials signed a Memorandum of Agreement for loans totaling PHP 1.5 million (PHP 100,000 each for 15 officials) from the unexpended municipal building fund. The loans were "purposely to purchase service vehicle for official use," payable in three years by payroll deduction. The SB passed, and Reyes approved, two resolutions both numbered 38-2003 (one describing the loans as for buying motor vehicles, the other as "livelihood projects") and Resolution No. 126-2003 requesting the mayor and the treasurer to release PHP 1.6 million to Loreto Transport Services Association, Inc. (LOTSA). On July 1, 2003, Treasurer Salise wrote Land Bank, with Reyes's approval, to transfer PHP 1.6 million from the municipality's account to LOTSA's account, and the bank did so. All the accused except Julao obtained loans.

After complaints reached the Ombudsman for Mindanao, Lorete recommended terminating them. A COA Special Audit Team found instead that the municipality disbursed PHP 1.6 million to LOTSA, a private entity composed of municipal officials and employees, as loans for vehicles for personal use. It found the release was by debit advice without disbursement vouchers or LOTSA's receipt, was recorded in the books only in 2004, and that only PHP 735,811.10 had been repaid as of March 2007, leaving PHP 864,188.90 unpaid. Reyes and the SB members were charged with violating Section 3(e) of RA 3019 "through evident bad faith and manifest partiality" (SB-10-CRM-0127). Reyes and Salise were also charged with malversation (SB-10-CRM-0128). The cases against Salise were dismissed on his death.

The Sandiganbayan convicted all the accused of violating Section 3(e) and Reyes of malversation. It rejected the good-faith defense because the accused "should have known better than to rely on the verbal affirmation (albeit erroneous) of a COA auditor." Their motions for reconsideration were denied, and they appealed. Estil did not appeal.
issues: Whether accused-appellants are guilty beyond reasonable doubt of violating Section 3(e) of RA 3019.
Whether Reyes is guilty beyond reasonable doubt of malversation of public funds.
ruling:
**1. No. The accused-appellants were acquitted because evident bad faith was not proved.** The first element (public officers discharging official functions) was undisputed. On the second, the Court noted *Villanueva v. COA*: reliance on a COA representative's expertise is a matter of defense in the criminal case, although the COA is not estopped from questioning its officials' acts on post-audit, since estoppel does not lie against the government. The trial record showed that the accused "may have been misled" by Lorete's erroneous opinion; the Sandiganbayan justice himself told Lorete, "Probably you gave them a wrong advice." The Court asked: "If accused-appellants could not reasonably rely on the opinion of Lorete, who is presumed to possess expertise in auditing financial transactions of government entities, and considering that the Municipality had no legal officer at the time, on whose opinion could they rely?" That the opinion was verbal and given before audit did not matter, because Lorete affirmed he gave it as one of his functions. The accused "had every right to presume that he not only performed his functions regularly but also correctly." The prosecution's theory that the consultation was a "mere subterfuge" was speculative. Even if bad faith attended it, the law requires *evident* bad faith. **The Sandiganbayan's remark that the accused "should have known better" revealed "ignorance rather than bad faith," unlike a case where the accused knew better but deliberately chose otherwise.** The Sandiganbayan made no finding of manifest partiality, and the Information did not allege gross inexcusable negligence; these modalities must be alleged with particularity. Since the second element was absent, the Court did not reach the third.

**2. Yes. Reyes is guilty of malversation.** The elements are: (1) the offender is a public officer; (2) he had custody or control of the funds by reason of his office; (3) the funds were public funds for which he was accountable; and (4) he appropriated, took or misappropriated them, or consented to or, through abandonment or negligence, permitted another person to take them. As mayor, Reyes is by law immediately and primarily responsible for all government funds and property of his agency. Under Article 217, as amended by RA 1060, the State need not prove actual misappropriation: failure to have the funds forthcoming upon demand raises a presumption of law that shifts the burden to the accused. **Even assuming the loans were meant for a public use, Reyes, as the accountable officer, failed to account for the funds, and "no proof was adduced to show that said loans were indeed applied for said public purpose."** The Court refused to "simply rely on the MOA and SB Resolutions and presume that the recipients of the loans purchased motorcycles to be used exclusively as official service vehicles." It also found it "most irregular" that the municipality lent money to its officials to buy service vehicles instead of procuring the vehicles itself. Reyes "utterly failed to rebut the statutory presumption of malversation."
disposition: The appeal was PARTLY GRANTED. The Sandiganbayan's September 28, 2018 Decision and March 28, 2019 Resolution were AFFIRMED in Criminal Case No. SB-10-CRM-0128: Reyes was found GUILTY of malversation of public funds and sentenced to an indeterminate penalty of six years and one day of prision mayor, as minimum, to 10 years of prision mayor, as maximum, with perpetual special disqualification and a fine of PHP 1.6 million. They were MODIFIED in Criminal Case No. SB-10-CRM-0127: Reyes, Daday, Gomez, Plaza, Magadan and Julao were ACQUITTED of violating Section 3(e) of RA 3019 on reasonable doubt, with entry of judgment to issue immediately as to them.

bar_questions.q: Mayor Ramon approved the transfer of PHP 2 million from the municipal general fund to a private association formed by municipal employees. The transfer was based on a sanggunian resolution and a memorandum of agreement stating that the money would be lent to municipal officials "exclusively to purchase service vehicles for official use," repayable through payroll deductions. Years later, a COA special audit found that a large balance remained unpaid. Charged with malversation, Ramon presented only the resolution and the agreement to show that the funds were intended for a public purpose. He presented no evidence that any vehicle was bought or used for official business. Has Ramon rebutted the presumption of malversation?

alac.answer: No. Ramon has not rebutted the presumption, and he may be convicted of malversation.
alac.legal_basis: Under the last paragraph of Article 217 of the Revised Penal Code, an accountable public officer's failure to have public funds duly forthcoming upon demand by a duly authorized officer is prima facie evidence that he put the funds to personal use. This presumption of law shifts the burden to the accused to rebut it with satisfactory evidence. A municipal mayor is immediately and primarily responsible for all government funds of his municipality. Notwithstanding the stated purpose or intention for public funds to be applied for a public purpose, the presumption remains unrebutted absent proof that the funds were actually applied for that purpose. (People v. Reyes, G.R. Nos. 246783-84, July 29, 2025)
alac.application: Ramon is an accountable officer who approved the release of PHP 2 million in municipal funds, and the audit showed the funds were not fully accounted for. His only evidence is the resolution and the agreement, which state what the money was intended for, not what it was actually used for. As in Reyes, a court cannot simply presume from those documents that the borrowers bought vehicles and used them only for official business. He offered no proof of actual application to a public purpose, so the burden that shifted to him was not discharged.
alac.conclusion: The statutory presumption of malversation stands unrebutted, and Ramon may be convicted of malversation of public funds.

bar_questions.q: Lacking a legal officer, the sanggunian members of a municipality asked the resident COA auditor whether they could realign the idle balance of a suspended infrastructure project into salary loans for officials. The auditor verbally opined that it was legal if supported by a sanggunian resolution. They passed the resolution and released the loans. Later audits found the scheme irregular. The Information for violation of Section 3(e) of RA 3019 alleged only "evident bad faith and manifest partiality." The Sandiganbayan convicted them, ruling that they "should have known better" than to rely on a verbal opinion, and made no finding of manifest partiality. (a) Did the accused act with evident bad faith? (b) May the Sandiganbayan instead convict them for gross inexcusable negligence?

alac.answer: (a) No, evident bad faith was not established. (b) No, gross inexcusable negligence was not alleged in the Information.
alac.legal_basis: Section 3(e) of RA 3019 requires that the public officer acted with manifest partiality, evident bad faith, or gross inexcusable negligence. Mere bad faith or partiality and negligence per se are not enough. Evident bad faith connotes a palpably and patently fraudulent and dishonest purpose to do moral obliquity or conscious wrongdoing for some perverse motive or ill will, not mere bad judgment. These modalities must be alleged with particularity in the Information. In People v. Reyes (G.R. Nos. 246783-84, July 29, 2025), the Court acquitted local officials who relied on the resident COA auditor's verbal opinion, holding that the finding that they "should have known better" showed ignorance rather than bad faith.
alac.application: (a) The officials had no legal officer and consulted the official presumed to have expertise in government financial transactions. They could presume that the auditor performed his functions regularly and correctly; that his opinion was verbal and given before audit does not matter. Saying they "should have known better" describes ignorance, not a conscious and deliberate wrongdoing driven by ill motive. (b) The Information alleged only evident bad faith and manifest partiality. Convicting them on gross inexcusable negligence, which was not alleged, would deprive them of their right to be informed of the charge. With no finding of manifest partiality, the second element of Section 3(e) is not proved.
alac.conclusion: The accused must be acquitted of violating Section 3(e) because evident bad faith was not proved, manifest partiality was not found, and gross inexcusable negligence was not alleged.

bar_questions.q: A provincial government released funds after its resident COA auditor verbally assured the governor that the transaction was proper. On post-audit, a COA special audit team found the release irregular and recommended charges. The governor argues that the COA is estopped from questioning a transaction that its own auditor had cleared. Is the governor correct?

alac.answer: No. The COA is not estopped from questioning, on post-audit, a transaction that its own auditor earlier cleared.
alac.legal_basis: Estoppel does not lie against the government, more so when the acts of its officials are erroneous or irregular. The COA is therefore not estopped from questioning, in post-audit, the previous acts of its officials. Reliance on the expertise of a COA representative is instead a matter of defense in the criminal case. (Villanueva v. Commission on Audit, as applied in People v. Reyes, G.R. Nos. 246783-84, July 29, 2025)
alac.application: The auditor's verbal clearance cannot bind the government or bar the COA's special audit team from finding the release irregular. At most, the governor may invoke his reliance on the auditor in a criminal prosecution, where good faith may negate evident bad faith under Section 3(e) of RA 3019, as in Reyes. That defense does not prevent the audit itself.
alac.conclusion: The governor's estoppel argument fails, though his reliance on the auditor may be raised as a defense in any criminal case.

notes: Accused Estil did not appeal; the Appellants' Brief alleges he died while the case was pending. He is not named in the acquittal, and the decision does not discuss whether the acquittal benefits him. The cases against Treasurer Salise were dismissed on August 22, 2017 on account of his death, although the decision's summary of the Sandiganbayan ruling says the Sandiganbayan "found Reyes and Salise guilty" of malversation. One sentence in that summary is garbled in the source ("It ruled that the failed to account for the funds"). The decision does not separately discuss the demand element; the Sandiganbayan found the accused failed to account after being presented with the COA audit observation.
